There's a difference between choosing to stay involved in your engineering business and the business needing you to be there.

Plenty of owners enjoy the work they started with: the shop floor, a difficult technical problem, a long-standing customer. I've known an owner who could tell from the sound of the shop floor when something wasn't running as it should, and I wouldn't ask anyone to give that up.

The question is what happens when you're away. If quotes wait for you, if quality depends on your walk round to catch what the inspection regime misses, or if your biggest customer will only talk to you, the involvement has stopped being a choice. It limits your freedom and can reduce the value of the business, because a buyer will want to know whether it can keep performing without you.

A useful test is to imagine four weeks away with no calls or emails and list what would suffer. That list tells you where the business still depends on you. Once you've dealt with those, you can decide which parts of the job you'd like to keep.
